items.raw: Multiple vulnerabilities have been discovered in SAP Products, the most severe of which could allow for arbitrary code execution. SAP NetWeaver is SAP’s technology platform and application server stack (ABAP and Java) that underpins many SAP business applications, including ERP and S/4HANA. SAP Web Dispatcher is a software load balancer and reverse proxy that receives web requests from the internet and forwards them to SAP application servers. SAP Gateway is the component that exposes SAP data and business logic through OData services and manages RFC communication between SAP systems and external applications. SAP ABAP Developer Tools is an eclipse-based development environment for writing, testing, and debugging ABAP code in SAP systems. S4CRM is the customer relationship management software for SAP S/4HANA, covering sales, service, and marketing processes. SAP Cloud SDK is a set of developer libraries (for languages such as Python and JavaScript) that simplify building applications that connect to SAP cloud services and AI capabilities. Successful exploitation of the most severe of these vulnerabilities could allow the attacker to execute arbitrary code and fully compromise the system, resulting in a high impact on confidentiality, integrity and availability of the system.

items.title: Trump taps Palantir security chief to run battered US cyber defense agency
items.summary: Michael LoSapio could inherit a depleted workforce and a political headache or two, courtesy of his current employer
items.raw: President Donald Trump has nominated Palantir security chief Michael LoSapio to lead CISA, putting an executive from the controversial government supplier in line to run America's civilian cyber defense agency. The nomination, announced on Monday, could end CISA's nearly two-year wait for a Senate-confirmed director following Jen Easterly's departure in January 2025. LoSapio has served as Palantir's CISO since September 2024, having previously led the company's infrastructure and network security team. He first joined the data analytics outfit in 2013, later spent a spell at database company SingleStore, and returned to Palantir in 2017. If confirmed, LoSapio would move from securing Palantir's systems to leading the federal government's main civilian cyber defense agency. CISA protects federal civilian networks and works with critical infrastructure operators, including power, water, and telecommunications providers. It's a substantial job, particularly given the state of the agency he would inherit. CISA has shed more than 1,000 staff, roughly a third of its workforce, since Trump returned to the White House, according to reports. It's now trying to plug the gaps, although acting director Nick Andersen said in September that around 250 would-be recruits were still waiting for security clearance before they could get to work. Andersen has been running CISA since February. With fewer people to go around, CISA is also rethinking where to spend its time. A strategy published last month emphasizes infrastructure whose failure would do the most damage, raising questions about what gets less attention as the agency operates with fewer staff. LoSapio would be the second person Trump has put forward for the role. His previous pick, Sean Plankey, withdrew in April after spending more than a year awaiting confirmation, with his nomination becoming caught up in a dispute involving Republican Senator Rick Scott over Coast Guard contracting. The nomination arrives late in the congressional calendar. If the Senate does not confirm LoSapio before the current Congress ends, Trump would have to nominate him again for consideration by the incoming Democratic-controlled Senate. Palantir, co-founded by billionaire Peter Thiel, has become a major supplier of technology to US government agencies, including the Department of Homeland Security and Immigration and Customs Enforcement (ICE). Its work with immigration authorities has attracted criticism from civil liberties groups

items.title: Vazamento em parceira da Sega expõe 2,2 milhões de endereços de email
items.summary: Usuários cadastrados em newsletters e outros serviços podem ter sido vítimas do vazamento.
items.raw: A desenvolvedora de games Sega revelou que foi vítima de um vazamento de dados a partir da invasão contra uma parceira terceirizada. Ao todo, aproximadamente 2,2 milhões de clientes da companhia foram afetados . Apenas o endereço de email das pessoas teria sido obtido pelo acesso não autorizado. De acordo com a própria companhia, informações pessoais, cadastrais ou financeiras não foram expostas . O caso envolve consumidores que estavam cadastrados em serviços de comunicação da marca, como newsletters. O hack explorou vulnerabilidades nos servidores da Arara , uma empresa também japonesa especializada em entrega de emails. Usuários cadastrados em newsletters e outros serviços podem ter sido vítimas do vazamento. Foto: Sega/Divulgação Para além dos 2,2 milhões de emails de clientes, foram obtidos também mais de 77 milhões de endereços de cerca de 380 clientes corporativos. A linha do tempo do vazamento da Sega De acordo com o comunicado oficial , o incidente aconteceu por “ vulnerabilidades em servidores web” e no ambiente de sistemas . Porém, não foram revelados detalhes da invasão e nem a autoria do hack. A empresa Arara divulgou oficialmente em 29 de outubro que foi vítima de um acesso não autorizado nos servidores , realizado um dia antes; No dia 31 de outubro, ela suspendeu o serviço de distribuição Arara Message , muito possivelmente o mais afetado na invasão; Porém, foi apenas em 2 de novembro que a dona da Arara, a Paycloud Holdings, falou especificamente sobre a quantidade de usuários afetados e notificou também as próprias clientes ; A Sega, por sua vez, emitiu o comunicado oficial de que foi uma das companhias atingidas quase uma semana depois , em 9 de novembro. A companhia também revelou que os invasores usaram o serviço de envio de mail para disparar mais de 7 milhões de mensagens falsas , fingindo ser um comunicado de empresas de cartão de crédito. Até por isso, ela pede que o consumidor tenha cuidado redobrado com futuras mensagens enviadas em nome da companhia — em especial aquelas com links suspeitos. Segundo incidente não relacionado Em um incidente aparentemente não relacionado, a Sega Fave, divisão de brinquedos, eletrônicos e arcades da marca, também teve um acesso não autorizado aos próprios servidores . Ela suspendeu atividades online e de cadastro envolvendo a Sega ID por tempo limitado, garantindo que não há evidências de roubo de dados. items.raw: A public iOS sandbox escape could expose wallet keys, Binance warns. No attacks are reported and no fix is confirmed. On 10 November, Binance warned users about a public iOS sandbox escape that lets one app read the files of other apps. Seed phrases, private keys and login credentials could be exposed to a malicious app, the exchange said. “A vulnerability (worse_query) affecting iOS 26.7.1, 27.0.1, and 27.2 allows malicious apps to read local files from other apps, putting seed phrases, private keys, and login credentials at risk across the entire ecosystem. This is an iOS-level issue, not unique to Binance.” reads the warning. Binance advises users to remove apps installed from untrusted sources, update iOS and all apps to the latest official versions, and, if a breach is suspected, move funds to a new wallet on a clean device and reset all active login sessions. A vulnerability (worse_query) affecting iOS 26.7.1, 27.0.1, and 27.2 allows malicious apps to read local files from other apps, putting seed phrases, private keys, and login credentials at risk across the entire ecosystem. This is an iOS-level issue, not unique to Binance.… — Binance (@binance) November 10, 2026 A researcher known as ‘forcequitOS’ published the PoC exploit code , called worse_query, on GitHub. Apple released security updates for both iOS versions the following day, but its release notes mysteriously don’t report a fix for the issue. The good news is that neither Binance nor the researcher has reported any attacks or data theft. “worse_query is the direct successor to bad_query and essentially replaces it. To use worse_query, you’ll have to set up an App Group container for your app.” forcequitOS wrote. The proof-of-concept can access the data folders used by all apps and, on iOS 27, some system folders as well. To work, an app must create an App Group container. The researcher says the code is intended for developers and “isn’t useful by itself.” However, other developers have already used it to build apps that can be installed on iPhones. One example is WQ Files , a file manager developed by Christoph Kolbicz, TheHackerNews reports . “ WQ Files is a file browser, app data manager and cache cleaner for iOS 26 and 27. “WQ” stands for worse_query, the sandbox technique it is built on. It reaches other apps’ and system containers with no jailbreak and no kernel exploit. Tested on iOS 26.7.1, 27.0.1 and 27.2.” reads the description . items.title: Fireworks AI gets burned twice as customer data exposure widens
items.summary: Inference biz pins latest breach on cloud provider and LLMJacking miscreants
items.raw: Fireworks AI has disclosed another cyberattack in October and a wider customer data exposure involving billing records, datasets, and incomplete model weights. The company, which lets customers train and run AI models, said a third-party cloud provider hosting its research and development machines was compromised on October 23. Attackers used that access the following day to reach Fireworks development systems and run an unauthorized workload. Fireworks suspects links to financially motivated criminals involved in LLMJacking – selling unauthorized access to AI models through illicit gateways. Fireworks grouped the affected data into three categories: Resource metadata: Resource identifiers, display names, descriptions, creation times, and more Billing information: Billing and shipping addresses, invoice and payment histories, account balances, and credit usages. Payment card numbers are not saved and therefore unaffected Model weights and datasets: For certain customers, a subset of incomplete model weights and datasets were accessed, Fireworks said Lin Qiao, Fireworks co-founder and CEO, said the apparent motive was not stealing model weights in response to concerns raised by Cantina Security CEO Hari Mulackal. "From what we see attackers are not after weights," said Qiao. "Most downloads were partial and stopped." Render founder and CEO Anurag Goel shared a notification from Notion warning that some chats with its AI assistant may have been exposed through the Fireworks incident. items.title: Researcher bypassed Meta smart glasses’ safeguards to run her own code
items.summary: She was able to bypass a safeguard meant to stop unauthorized software running on Meta glasses. It wasn't easy, but showed it is possible.
items.raw: We’ve written before about what Meta’s Ray-Ban smart glasses can see and hear , and who might get to use that information. Those worries focus on how the glasses handle information during normal use. A security researcher has now shown how to bypass a safeguard meant to stop unauthorized software running on them. Vulnerability researcher Paula, known online as pamoutaf, found a way to run her own software on a pair of Ray-Ban Meta glasses. For the technical details I’ll gladly refer you to her own post about it. The glasses are controlled by the Meta AI app on the owner’s phone. Developers can add their own apps to the glasses through a developer tool, and the phone sends that software to the glasses to install. The glasses were supposed to check that the software really came from Meta. In older firmware (up to and including version 126), they didn’t check, so the researcher could swap in an app of her own. Meta introduced a check in firmware version 127 to verify the app’s digital signature to prove that it came from Meta . The researcher found the on/off switch for that signature check came from a settings file passed along by the phone. The glasses only checked the file was correctly formed, not whether it had been tampered with. Changing a single byte in the file turned the signature check off. Once her app was running, she could send commands to the glasses from the paired phone over a wireless connection. The glasses have a camera, microphones and a wireless connection, and they sit on your face all day. A wearable that can be made to run unapproved code goes beyond a privacy-policy question. It becomes a security question about who controls the device. As we’ve seen, some cheaper smart glasses already are a security disaster . In this case the person running the code would be the person that controls the phone. If malicious software running on the glasses could access the camera or stored recordings, it could potentially send footage to an attacker’s server. Pamoutaf’s research doesn’t demonstrate that scenario, but it raises questions about what that software might be able to access. In her post she promised a follow-up exploring other potential ways to attack the glasses. How to stay safe Keep the glasses’ firmware and the Meta AI app updated, and avoid unofficial apps or modifications. If smart glasses are just another gadget to you, I’d leave them on the shelf. items.title: Avião é evacuado nos EUA após conversa sobre Call of Duty gerar alerta de bomba
items.summary: Após a inspeção da aeronave, os passageiros retornaram e o voo decolou sem maiores problemas.
items.raw: Um voo que aguardava a autorização para decolar no Aeroporto Internacional de Ontario, na Califórnia (Estados Unidos), precisou ser evacuado após uma conversa sobre o jogo Call of Duty acabar confundida com uma ameaça de bomba . O fato inusitado aconteceu no último último domingo (8). Segundo a CBS News , um passageiro ouviu outra pessoa que estava na aeronave da Frontier Airlines mencionar as palavras “bomba” e “explosão” e alertou imediatamente a tripulação. Por precaução, os funcionários da companhia aérea acionaram as autoridades policiais, que decidiram investigar a denúncia. Nenhuma bomba localizada A partir do chamado, os policiais foram ao avião e iniciaram o protocolo de segurança para investigar a possibilidade de bomba . Como medida preventiva, todos os passageiros tiveram que sair da aeronave e a evacuação também atingiu a ala leste do Terminal 2 do aeroporto californiano . Durante a ação, o passageiro responsável pelos comentários que levaram ao alerta de bomba foi detido e interrogado, mas rapidamente esclareceu a situação; Prestando depoimento às autoridades, ele afirmou que estava em uma videochamada enquanto aguardava a decolagem ; Conforme o suspeito, as referências a bombas e explosões faziam parte de eventos relacionados ao jogo Call of Duty , que motivaram a conversa via FaceTime ; Mesmo assim, os policiais realizaram uma varredura na parte interna do avião e na área de embarque do aeroporto. O trabalho foi finalizado sem que nenhuma bomba fosse encontrada , como detalhou a reportagem. Com as autoridades concluindo que não houve crime, todos os passageiros reembarcaram no avião, incluindo o homem cujos comentários levaram ao incidente, e o voo decolou normalmente para o destino não revelado. Curiosamente, a famosa franquia dos games já motivou outros incidentes semelhantes . Em um deles, a Polícia da Flórida invadiu uma casa após vizinhos relatarem discussões sobre armas e barulhos de tiros, acreditando se tratar de violência doméstica, mas os moradores estavam apenas empolgados jogando Call of Duty , segundo o site Dexerto . Siga no TecMundo e confira o review de Call of Duty: Modern Warfare 4 , lançamento mais recente da série. Com informações de CBS News e Dexerto .

items.raw: Overview On November 9, 2026, N-able announced that it was responding to the public disclosure of critical vulnerabilities affecting N-central , its remote monitoring and management (RMM) platform. In a public disclosure titled Able2Shell, an independent researcher has published details and proof-of-concept (PoC) code covering 33 issues. According to the disclosure, the issues include unauthenticated remote code execution (RCE), privilege escalation to root, credential disclosure, and unauthorized account creation. One unauthenticated chain combines XML external entity (XXE) and session-handling weaknesses to execute code as the nable service account. Other demonstrated chains involve an administrator viewing malicious patch metadata or use ProductAdmin credentials. Rapid7 Intelligence is currently triaging the newly published details. As of November 10, N-able reported scanning activity associated with the published PoC code and said it had no evidence that any customer environment had been successfully exploited. The vendor has advised keeping N-central deployments offline while it develops and validates a hotfix. Hosted N-central classic environments remain offline, according to the same notice. N-able's notice does not yet include CVE identifiers or CVSS scores. N-central is used by managed service providers (MSPs) and enterprise IT teams to administer endpoints and infrastructure. Compromise of an RMM server can put downstream managed environments at risk. N-central has previously been targeted through separate vulnerabilities, including an authentication bypass covered by Rapid7 in August 2026 . Given the platform's administrative reach and the availability of public exploit code, Rapid7 recommends treating the current disclosure as an emergency. Mitigation guidance Rapid7 strongly recommends that organizations operating on-premises N-central servers take them offline immediately and keep them offline until the hotfix is available , and the server has been successfully upgraded. Hosted customers should follow the vendor's service restoration updates. N-able is developing and validating a hotfix, with a target of midday November 10 EST. Affected versions: The researcher reports testing N-central Appliance 2026.4.0.31 . N-able's current notice does not specify the full affected-version range. items.raw: Your managed detection and response (MDR) provider flags suspicious activity, and your analyst spends the next hour finding the account, checking logs, and deciding whether anything needs to happen. By the time the investigation is underway, the alert feels less like help and more like a task assignment. MDR should bring your team capacity and expertise when it needs them. If the service keeps handing the hardest work back to your analysts, these five signs can help you work out where the arrangement is falling short. 1. Every alert arrives with homework If your analysts are still sorting through the same recurring false positives, the extra coverage may be creating more work than it removes. Even an alert worth investigating is only so useful when your team has to gather the basic context before it can make a decision. Take a few recent alerts and look at what your provider had already checked when it contacted you. You should be able to see how it separated routine activity from a credible threat, and what it did to stop familiar noise from coming back. 2. It spots the fire, but cannot see the fuel A suspicious login involving an account with broad access deserves a different response from the same activity on a tightly restricted account. The systems within reach, their importance to the business, and any known weaknesses all help determine what needs attention first. When your MDR leaves your team to assemble that picture during an investigation, valuable time goes into finding context that could have informed the response from the start. Find out how your provider uses information about assets, identities, vulnerabilities, and current threats, including what it can help you address before an incident occurs. 3. Your team gets incident updates, but few useful lessons When a provider contains a threat and closes the case, your team should come away with more than a record of what happened. Consider the last significant investigation: did it lead to a clearer detection, a stronger response plan, or a better understanding of how an attacker moved through your environment? If similar activity appears three months later and your analysts have to work through the same questions, the service has missed a chance to make them better prepared. Expertise is most useful when your team can apply some of it next time. 4. items.summary: Key Points Introduction Over the past year, Check Point Research investigated a series of intrusion campaigns targeting several dozens of high-profile organizations across Latin America, Asia, and Europe. However, we identified numerous connections between the tools and their […]
items.raw: Key Points During a year-long investigation, Check Point Research identified three distinct operational clusters spanning Latin America, Asia, and Europe targeting telecommunications providers, government organizations, military entities, research institutions, and critical infrastructure. The clusters , SilentDelivery, OceanGate and DarkWire , are linked through shared infrastructure features and malware code similarities within the Sparrow malware framework. We track the entity behind the Sparrow framework as CopperDragon , a potential digital quartermaster supporting China-nexus threat actors, including FamousSparrow , Earth Estries , TropicTrooper , UAT-9244 , and others. Each cluster employed a different toolset and different initial access techniques, including compromising internet-facing infrastructure and highly selective watering-hole attacks. The compromised websites that were used for watering hole attacks were of government, shipping, and IT and research sectors. Our research uncovered several previously undocumented tools and new details about the Sparrow framework, including Windows and Linux variants, passive backdoor capabilities , and a connection to the Melofee backdoor. Introduction Over the past year, Check Point Research investigated a series of intrusion campaigns targeting several dozens of high-profile organizations across Latin America, Asia, and Europe. These campaigns initially appeared to be independent operations, each using different backdoors, post-exploitation tools and operational pace. However, we identified numerous connections between the tools and their infrastructure which linked them to the same Sparrow malware ecosystem. We track the entity behind these campaigns as CopperDragon , which may serve as a digital quartermaster supporting a number of China-nexus threat actors that use the Sparrow cross-platform malware framework for Linux and Windows. What is CopperDragon? FamousSparrow is a threat actor that was first identified in 2021, whose main backdoor is SparrowDoor . Since then, multiple vendors have reported on related activity and malware variants, including CrowDoor , HemiGate , and TernDoor . Over time, it became apparent that this other activity was not necessarily carried out by the original FamousSparrow group. items.title: Chrome zero-day whack-a-mole continues as 2026 tally hits 8
items.summary: Another Chrome memory bug gets squashed, but not before attackers got their hands on it
items.raw: Google has patched its eighth actively exploited Chrome zero-day of 2026, matching its total for the whole of last year with nearly two months still left on the calendar. The latest flaw, tracked as CVE-2026-125350, is a high-severity use-after-free vulnerability in Chrome's XML component. Google confirmed in a security advisory published Monday that attackers are already exploiting the bug, although it hasn't said who's behind the attacks or who might be getting targeted. "Google is aware that an exploit for CVE-2026-125350 exists in the wild," the company said, offering little else about the attacks. The vulnerability was reported anonymously on November 6 and involves a memory management error that occurs when software continues using a pointer to memory that has already been freed. Such bugs can potentially allow attackers to corrupt memory and execute malicious code, although Google hasn't disclosed how this particular flaw is being exploited. Google is keeping further technical details under wraps until enough users have installed the fix, a familiar approach intended to stop other attackers from getting their hands on a working exploit. The patch arrives in Chrome 157.0.8103.50/.51 for Windows and macOS, and 157.0.8103.50 for Linux. The update also addresses eight other security vulnerabilities, including high-severity flaws affecting WebGL, FileSystem, GPU, Compositing, and the V8 JavaScript engine. The release fixes another use-after-free bug in Chrome's XML component, CVE-2026-125346, which was reported by Arni Hardarson of Neonix Security in October, though Google hasn't indicated that this second vulnerability is being exploited. The latest discovery adds to what's becoming a rather long list of Chrome zero-days this year. By June, Google had already patched five actively exploited Chrome zero-days, including flaws in its V8 JavaScript engine, Skia graphics library, and WebGPU implementation. The list has only grown since then, with two more V8 bugs fixed in September and the latest XML vulnerability bringing the total to eight. That puts 2026 level with 2025, when Google also fixed eight Chrome zero-days exploited in the wild. Whether the browser maker can make it through the remaining weeks of the year without adding another to the pile is anyone's guess. items.summary: Google has released Chrome updates for desktop and Android to patch a zero-day vulnerability already being exploited in attacks.
items.raw: On November 9, Google issued a security update to Chrome’s Stable channel for Windows, Mac, and Linux. The update is rolling out over the coming days and weeks. Most users are on Chrome’s Stable channel. The desktop update brings Chrome to versions 157.0.8103.50/.51 for Windows and Mac and 157.0.8103.50 for Linux . It includes nine security fixes, including one for an actively exploited zero-day vulnerability. A zero-day vulnerability is a security flaw disclosed or exploited before an official fix becomes available. Hong Kong’s Computer Emergency Response Team Coordination Centre (HKCERT) rates the overall risk as “Extremely High.” Its bulletin says some of the vulnerabilities address in the update could allow denial of service, security restriction bypass, and remote code execution. How to update Chrome The easiest option is to allow Chrome to update automatically. But you can end up lagging behind on updates if you never close your browser or if something goes wrong, such as an extension preventing the update. If you don’t want to wait for the rollout to reach you, you can update manually. Open About Google Chrome from Chrome’s Settings or Help menu. Chrome will check for updates and download any available update. If prompted, click Relaunch to apply it. Chrome 157.0.8103.51 is up to date You can find an explanation of the version numbering system and step-by-step instructions in our guide: How to update Chrome on every operating system . Google also released Chrome 157.0.8103.50 for Android on November 9. Google says it includes the same security fixes as the desktop release unless otherwise noted. Android users should check Google Play for the update. Technical details Let’s take a closer look at that zero-day vulnerability. Google says it was notified about a vulnerability by an unnamed third party on November 6. The vulnerability is tracked as CVE-2026-125350 and rated as a high-severity use-after-free vulnerability in Chrome’s XML component. XML is a data format Chrome uses to read and process certain kinds of structured web content. XML stands for Extensible Markup Language: it labels information with tags, rather like HTML, but allows authors to define their own tags to describe their data. items.title: Ransomware threat blares from Vanderbilt University computers during cyberattack
items.summary: BYOD claims extensive data theft as campus Wi-Fi returns, most systems remain restricted, and classes carry on
items.raw: Classes at Vanderbilt University are proceeding as scheduled today, although access to most university systems remains restricted following a cyberattack claimed by ransomware group BYOD. Vanderbilt announced on Monday morning that it was dealing with "an active cybersecurity incident," and that the fallout may affect university devices, systems, and cloud-based services. The Nashville-based university initially told students and staff to shut down university devices and disconnect from campus Wi-Fi. It warned them to watch for unexpected prompts, altered files or permissions, unfamiliar applications, and unsolicited authentication requests. Campus computers reportedly began playing an audio threat attributed to BYOD. Student newspaper The Vanderbilt Hustler cited posts on campus social network Fizz showing the message. "You have been compromised by BYOD," the recording said. "We suggest you reach out to us as soon as possible. Instructions have been placed on your desktop. Failure to communicate will result in this estate being brought to the ground completely. Make the right choice or rot with the wrong one." By Monday evening, Vanderbilt had restored access to campus Wi-Fi, but warned that access to most systems remains restricted. "We know this has disrupted important work and caused frustration across the university," it said. "Vanderbilt Information Technology is working with government agencies and other partners to manage this situation." Students were told to attend classes as scheduled on Tuesday and contact instructors about flexibility on coursework deadlines. Staff were instructed to report to work normally. Vanderbilt's Athletics department said that its ticketing system was unavailable, and that students were unable to claim tickets for the college's football game against Alabama on Saturday. BYOD claimed responsibility for the attack on Vanderbilt on Monday, along with extensive data theft. "If you could not tell already, your databases are locked [and] we have your entire estate and research data," it said via its leak site. "Over 1 million SSNs, full names, email addresses, phone numbers, student and employee records, full takeover of your DC, whatever was on your network, we possess." Vanderbilt has not confirmed BYOD's claims about the extent of its access or the data allegedly stolen. BYOD may be a familiar name to some. items.raw: Microsoft researchers have uncovered a memory-safety bug in Rust’s standard library that had gone undetected for nearly 11 years, alongside other flaws that can trigger undefined behavior even in applications written entirely in safe Rust. Two of the findings affect stable Rust, including a separate issue that could cause applications to access freed memory. The nearly 11-year-old bug involves Rust’s process::exit function. Microsoft’s FORGE Lab researchers found that calling the function from a child thread could cause the runtime to remove the main thread’s alternate signal stack while it was still running. If the main thread subsequently experienced a stack overflow, the operating system could be unable to deliver the signal correctly, resulting in a segmentation fault instead of Rust’s intended stack-overflow handling. “The process::exit signal stack bug was in the standard library for nearly 11 years,” the researchers wrote in a blog post . Microsoft said the researchers found no reliable exploitation path under the conditions they examined and assessed practical exploitation as unlikely. The research used Hyenas, FORGE Lab’s AI-powered vulnerability-scanning system, to investigate unsafe code in Rust’s standard library. Hyenas is the lab’s research version of codename MDASH, Microsoft’s agentic vulnerability-discovery system. Microsoft said some of the bugs were found with help from Hyenas. Researchers then examined the underlying code, reproduced the issues, assessed their security impact, and reported them to Rust maintainers. Microsoft said the practical risk is limited. Each flaw requires unusual conditions to trigger, and a bug in the standard library becomes “a serious vulnerability only if a real program reaches the API in that way,” the researchers wrote. Unsafe code challenges Rust’s safety guarantees Rust’s ownership model and type system are designed to prevent memory-safety problems commonly associated with languages such as C and C++. However, its standard library relies on unsafe code internally for operations that the compiler cannot verify. Components such as Vec and String use these operations but expose them through safe APIs. items.raw: An attacker has abused AWS cross-account IAM roles to access multiple customer environments, steal data, and harvest credentials in a supply-chain attack that ran between October 14 and October 26. Researchers from Wiz, working with Sentra and Mandiant, said they observed an attacker using IAM credentials for Qubole’s AWS account to assume roles in customer environments. The compromised credentials allowed the attacker to access customer AWS accounts that had previously established cross-account access permissions with Qubole. The access was used to enumerate cloud resources, retrieve secrets and configuration data, download files from Amazon S3 , and test credentials belonging to affected organizations. Sentra, which initially identified suspicious activity across several customer environments, said the campaign affected dozens of Qubole customers. The attacker was said to have exploited integrations that remained trusted even after some organizations had stopped using the platform. Attackers used Qubole’s AWS credentials Qubole integrations rely on cross-account Identity and Access Management ( IAM ) roles. Customers typically create roles that allow identities belonging to Qubole’s AWS account to assume them, with an External ID serving as an additional check against unauthorized access. The attacker had credentials that could satisfy this requirement. Wiz said the first suspicious activity was observed on October 14, when an IP address associated with Mullvad VPN attempted to assume customer integration roles from AWS account 805246085872, which Qubole uses for its platform operations. The requests used an IAM user identified as AIDA3W7DIFLYOLTK63SFS. Most of the activity that came later originated from an OVH-hosted VPS, 57.129.54[.]120. The attacker also began using a second IAM identity associated with Qubole’s AWS account on October 18, alongside another Mullvad VPN address. All malicious role-assumption requests identified by Wiz included the required External ID and succeeded. Many of the targeted roles had seen no legitimate Qubole activity during October, but their permissions remained active. After gaining access, the attacker enumerated cloud resources, including S3 buckets, databases, EC2 instances, security groups and IAM identities. The intruder also accessed AWS Secrets Manager, Systems Manager Parameter Store and Lambda function configurations to retrieve credentials and other sensitive information. items.title: Google DeepMind melds humans and AI agents to vet Signal's secure messaging techniques
items.summary: Post-quantum handshake and Triple Ratchet get a formal security check
items.raw: Google DeepMind researchers have completed a formal verification of Signal's messaging security, marking what they claim is the first time AI has helped devise a proof that links protocol-level security guarantees to a widely used cryptographic implementation. They did so using AlphaProof Code, a multi-agent framework for formal software specification and verification. AlphaProof Code relies on a human-guided agent that writes a Lean specification, assesses machine code semantics, and crafts an agent-authored proof that the Lean kernel checks against the specification. In this instance, AlphaProof Code verified Signal’s post-quantum PQXDH handshake and Triple Ratchet, thereby validating the design of libsignal's forward secrecy, authentication, post-compromise security, and handshake secrecy. In so doing, the Google/DeepMind team – Swarat Chaudhuri, Andrew Ferraiuolo, Anton Kovsharov, Tej Chajed, Sam Schlesinger, Karn Seth, Jonathan Katz, Charles Sutton, and Pushmeet Kohli – has taken a step toward a challenge the Beneficial AI Foundation issued in April to formally verify the Signal protocol and Signal app with Lean. The AlphaProof Code process involves working with various models to turn Signal's security goals into a human-reviewed mathematical specification. Based on this spec, the researchers assigned Gemini Carbon agents to generate Lean code proving the correctness of the libsignal implementation. After the agents generated 6.5 million lines of Lean code, they undertook an auditing pass and flagged bits that required human review. The result is theoretical in that it assumes perfect cryptography and doesn't guarantee the computational secrecy of bytes. But it's still a meaningful assertion of correctness. "It's a system that is fundamentally built for human AI collaboration," said Swarat Chaudhuri, research scientist at Google DeepMind and a professor at the University of Texas at Austin, in an interview with The Register. Traditionally, said Chaudhuri, you start proving theorems with well-defined problems formulated by a mathematician that get submitted to an AI agent for proof. In this case, the researchers had to figure out what to prove. "In formal methods, we always had this belief that verification is the hard bit," he said. "There's thirty or forty years of work on how to scale up verification. Now we are able to do that. items.title: Ex-agente do FBI desviou milhões de dólares roubados de crimes virtuais
items.summary: De acordo com o DOJ, as ações do ex-agente causaram um impacto significativo na segurança nacional
items.raw: Um ex-agente do FBI se declarou culpado por acusações de fraude eletrônica e lavagem de dinheiro após desviar quase US$ 2,5 milhões (mais de R$ 13 milhões em conversão direta) em criptomoedas. Patrick Steven Yaroch, de 37 anos, desviou o montante de carteiras digitais pertencentes a vítimas de fraudes e hackers investigados pela agência federal. Yaroch atuou no esquadrão de segurança nacional da divisão de Boston do FBI entre 2017 e 2025, e como agente especial supervisor na Divisão de Contrainteligência e Espionagem até meados de 2026. Ele foi preso em 31 de julho, após ter relatado o roubo dos ativos digitais à Divisão de Segurança Nacional (NSD), ao Departamento de Justiça (DOJ) e a funcionários do próprio FBI, em 29 de julho. Os documentos do processo apontam que o homem utilizou o seu acesso privilegiado aos sistemas de gerenciamento para obter senhas de recuperação de algumas carteiras digitais apreendidas. Com essas credenciais, Patrick conseguiu realizar cerca de 100 transferências ilícitas, afetando 35 investigações diferentes. Após drenar esses fundos para as suas próprias carteiras, o ex-agente do FBI tentou lavar o dinheiro convertendo esses ativos originais em outras criptomoedas. Entre novembro de 2025 e janeiro de 2026, Yaroch transferiu dezenas de milhares de dólares para contas bancárias pessoais . Ele utilizou o dinheiro para quitar dívidas, empréstimos e financiamento de veículos. De acordo com o DOJ, as ações do ex-agente causaram um impacto significativo na segurança nacional Foto: NBC Wasghinton/reprodução Plano de fuga com ChatGPT Os documentos sobre o caso ainda citam que Patrick Yaroch tinha um inusitado plano para abandonar os Estados Unidos e recomeçar sua vida na Europa, com auxílio do ChatGPT . O homem chegou a perguntar ao modelo de IA o que a tecnologia faria se “tivesse cerca de US$ 1 milhão (R$ 5,5 milhões) e quisesse deixar os EUA para se tornar residente ou cidadão de um país da União Europeia?”. A inteligência artificial até fez sugestões interessantes, baseadas na idade e no desejo do usuário em ter uma vida mais tranquila. Dentre as indicações estavam as regiões de vinícolas em Portugal. Isso levou o próprio Patrick a comprar passagens aéreas para Lisboa previstas para setembro e assinar documentos para obter um número de identificação fiscal português. items.title: Spyware attacks trend toward hitting just about anyone
items.summary: iVerify’s report Tuesday adds to evidence of spyware’s increasingly indiscriminate targeting.
items.raw: There’s mounting evidence of spyware attacks growing more indiscriminate, leading to more everyday citizens being hit as opposed to traditionally “high-value” targets. The AdFection spyware attacks , which could infect anyone visiting a website that had advertising on it, represented the most recent revelation. And iVerify published a report Tuesday analyzing customer infections and threat notifications from Apple that contributes to the trend. “Conventional guidance on spyware risk focused on people with a public profile, a sensitive job or a role that put them on a government’s radar,” the company said. “Some Apple Threat Notification cases iVerify saw this year don’t fit that pattern.” “In Ottawa, Apple Threat Notifications reached the children of a city bus driver and a stay-at-home mom,” it continued. “In Australia, one went to a limousine driver. None of them had a public profile, a sensitive job or an obvious connection to anyone worth spying on. These cases matter because they show the threat reaching people who had no reason to expect it. For an enterprise, the employees most likely to be hit look much more like the limousine driver than like the CEO.” Part of that is that when spyware attacks are less targeted, they might be more likely to hit those who aren’t as diligently focused on routine cyber hygiene, as opposed to CEOs who are probably regularly upgrading their defenses, iVerify told CyberScoop. Rocky Cole, co-founder of the company, said the change reflects a shift in who’s using spyware. “The vast majority of our detections were mass attacks by criminal groups looking to do purely criminal things,” Cole said. “For the purposes of stealing credentials and selling them on the black market, an executive credential is not necessarily more valuable than a system administrator or even an average employee.” iVerify’s report looked at other trends as well. Among the findings: iVerify didn’t see any devices that were infected by the DarkSword or Coruna iOS exploit kits where users received Apple threat notifications, suggesting that the tech giant might be overly focused on nation-state threats and well-known commercial mercenary spyware like NSO Group’s Pegasus. The rate of spyware infections held relatively steady in 2026, at 1.07 infections per 1,000 iOS consumer scans. “Three in four of this year’s detections were criminal adversaries stealing credentials and cryptocurrency, not state-sponsored actors,” the report said.

items.raw: Google patched nine Chrome flaws, including a V8 vulnerability tracked as CVE-2026-125350, that attackers have been actively exploiting in the wild. Google has addressed multiple security vulnerabilities, one of which, tracked as CVE-2026-125350, has been actively exploited in the wild. The vulnerability is a use after free issue that resides in XML and was reported by an anonymous source on November 6, 2026.. “Google is aware that an exploit for CVE-2026-125350 exists in the wild.” reads the advisory . A Use-after-free (UAF) is a memory corruption vulnerability that occurs when a program continues to use a piece of memory after it has been released (freed). In simple terms, an application allocates memory to store data, then releases that memory when it is no longer needed. A use-after-free bug occurs when the application later tries to access that same memory location, even though it is no longer valid. Attackers may exploit a use-after-free vulnerability to crash an application and cause a denial-of-service condition, corrupt memory, or, under certain conditions, execute arbitrary code. Depending on the affected component and the nature of the flaw, successful exploitation could also allow attackers to escalate their privileges. The IT giant has not shared further details about how attackers are exploiting the vulnerability or who is behind the attacks. “Access to bug details and links may be kept restricted until a majority of users are updated with a fix. We will also retain restrictions if the bug exists in a third party library that other projects similarly depend on, but haven’t yet fixed.” continues the advisory. CVE-2026-125350 is the eighth exploited Chrome zero-day of 2026. Since the start of the year, Google has addressed the following zero-day flaws exploited in attacks in the wild: February 2026 – CVE-2026-2441 (CVSS score: 8.8) – Use after free in CSS. March 2026 – CVE-2026-3909 (CVSS score: 8.8) – Out-of-bounds write in the Skia 2D graphics library and CVE-2026-3910 (CVSS score: 8.8) – Flaw in the implementation of the V8 JavaScript/WebAssembly engine. April 2026 – CVE-2026-5281 (CVSS score: 8.8) – Use-after-free bug in Dawn, the WebGPU component used for graphics processing. items.title: Russian Turla group used new toolset to silently pilfer emails from Kazakhstan, Romanian governments
items.summary: Nicknamed “Turla’s Cereal,” the tools target Microsoft Exchange servers and lack many obvious indicators of compromise or malicious telemetry, per a new ESET report.
items.raw: Turla, a notorious cyberespionage group aligned with the Russian government, has been wielding a new, customizable toolset to compromise governments around the world over the past year, including Kazakhstan. The toolset was first discovered in November 2025 by cybersecurity firm ESET, which named it “Turla’s Cereal” as a play on its highly modular, interconnected and “serialized” design. It chains and exploits different legitimate functions across Microsoft Exchange, Windows, and .NET assemblies, which Microsoft has described as “the fundamental units of deployment, version control, reuse, activation scoping, and security permissions for .NET-based applications.” “One of the most interesting aspects of this toolset is what we did not find: external command and control infrastructure,” ESET researcher Matías Porolli wrote in the report , released Tuesday. “Instead — adding insult to injury — the victim’s compromised Exchange server is co-opted to act as the C&C infrastructure.” Illustration of Turla’s Cereal compromise of Microsoft Exchange servers using a modular, stealthy toolset. (Source: ESET) Multiple Western governments and threat intelligence firms have attributed Turla as a part of Russia’s Federal Security Service (FSB), which is tasked with gathering intelligence on foreign governments, businesses and organizations. According to MITRE, the group has compromised victims in more than 50 countries, spanning governments, militaries, private-sector companies and research organizations. Porolli said the toolset was found on a compromised Exchange server used by the government of Kazakhstan on Nov. 28, 2025, where it could receive commands, execute in memory, gather intel on the organization and collect certain email messages. Another version found inside a Romanian government agency a month later was configured to target emails sent to or received by the Western powers — the European Union and the North Atlantic Treaty Organization — adversarial with Russia. At the time , Romanian politicians were calling for a NATO mission in the Black Sea to deter what they viewed as Russian aggression. In July, the EU announced sanctions against Russian individuals and organizations, citing a yearslong cyberespionage campaign from Turla and other Russian groups against European nations as well as the targeting of Poland’s energy grid and European businesses by Russia-aligned hacking groups. items.summary: A N-able retirou temporariamente o N-central do ar após a divulgação de mais de trinta vulnerabilidades do tipo zero-day por parte de um investigador. Estas falhas permitiam que agentes maliciosos executassem código remotamente, roubassem credenciais e criassem contas de administrador. O impacto afeta a estabilidade e a segurança dos sistemas geridos pela plataforma afetada.
points: A N-able colocou o N-central offline após a divulgação de mais de 30 zero-days.
Um investigador revelou falhas que permitiam execução remota de código e roubo de credenciais.
Os atacantes podiam criar contas de administrador nos sistemas vulneráveis.
items.why: Protege os utilizadores contra explorações ativas de dezenas de falhas críticas em ferramentas de gestão.
items.todo: Acompanhe os comunicados do fornecedor e suspenda o uso de serviços afetados até à correção.

items.title: IBM Aspera Faspex, SignalWire FreeSwitch Vulnerabilities Exploited in Attacks
items.summary: A CISA adicionou as vulnerabilidades CVE-2026-123218 e CVE-2026-116779 ao seu catálogo de explorações conhecidas devido a ataques ativos observados. A agência governamental emitiu um aviso a instar as agências federais a aplicarem as respetivas correções no prazo de três dias. Esta medida visa mitigar o impacto de explorações direcionadas a estes produtos.
points: A CISA adicionou CVE-2026-123218 e CVE-2026-116779 ao catálogo de falhas exploradas.
As vulnerabilidades afetam o IBM Aspera Faspex e o SignalWire FreeSwitch.
As agências federais foram instruídas a corrigir os problemas em três dias.
items.why: Alerta para falhas que estão a ser ativamente exploradas em ataques no mundo real.
items.todo: Atualize com urgência os softwares IBM Aspera Faspex e SignalWire FreeSwitch afetados.

items.title: Anthropic sharpens AI coding and security capabilities with Mythos 5.2
items.summary: A Anthropic lançou os novos modelos Claude Fable 5.2 e Mythos 5.2, prometendo melhorias significativas em tarefas de engenharia de software e reduções de preços face às versões anteriores. Enquanto o Fable 5.2 está amplamente disponível, o acesso ao Mythos é restrito a organizações de cibersegurança e ciências da vida para evitar utilizações maliciosas. Embora ofereçam um desempenho superior na geração de código e autonomia, persistem desafios relacionados com a fiabilidade sem supervisão humana.
points: A Anthropic lançou os modelos Fable 5.2 e Mythos 5.2 com melhor desempenho e preços mais baixos.
O acesso ao modelo Mythos está restrito a entidades vetadas para mitigar riscos de segurança.
Os novos modelos aumentam a velocidade e a capacidade na programação e tarefas complexas.
items.why: Mostra a evolução dos modelos de IA avançados e a necessidade de restringir o acesso a versões de alto risco.
items.todo: Avalie o rácio custo-eficácia e mantenha supervisão humana rigorosa ao integrar agentes de IA autónomos.
